title: Percent increase and decrease, discount, tax and tip
blurb: Find percent increase and decrease from the right base, price discounts, tax, tips and markups with multipliers, and undo a percent correctly.
question: A pair of scrubs is $80, marked 25% off, and then 8% sales tax is added at the register. Later the store raises the price from $50 back to $60. The HESI A2 asks for the amount paid and the percent increase. Which number do you divide by, and why can't you just add and subtract percents?

teach.h: Change compared with where you started
teach.body: Formally, percent change = (new value − original value) ÷ original value × 100%. A positive result is an increase; a negative result is a decrease. In plain English: find how much it changed, then ask 'what percent of the STARTING amount is that change?' The starting amount is always the base, which is why a rise from $40 to $50 and a fall from $50 to $40 are different percents.

steps.sub: Turn the decimal into a percent

teach.caption: Percent changes are not symmetric: the base is different each way.

teach.h: Use one multiplier for each change
teach.body: Instead of finding the discount and subtracting it, multiply by what is left. 25% off leaves 75%, so the sale price is original × 0.75. Adding 8% tax makes 108%, so the total is price × 1.08. A tip or commission on its own is bill × rate; a 40% markup gives selling price = cost × 1.40. Multipliers save a step, and they make multi-step problems simple: just multiply them in the order the story gives.

items: Ashley, a nursing student, buys $80 scrubs at 25% off, and 8% tax is charged on the sale price.
Ashley pays $64.80. (Tax is charged on the discounted price, the order the store applies them.)
If the price later goes from $50 to $60: change 10, base 50, 10 ÷ 50 = 0.20, a 20% increase.

teach.text: Successive percents MULTIPLY; they do not add. 20% off and then another 10% off is 0.80 × 0.90 = 0.72 of the price, a 28% total discount, not 30%. A 10% rise followed by a 10% fall gives 1.10 × 0.90 = 0.99: a 1% net LOSS, not 'back to the start'.

teach.caption: The second 10% is taken from $80, not from $100, so it removes only $8.

items: After a 20% discount a price is $64. The sale price is 80% of the original: original × 0.80 = 64.
Simple interest: I = P × r × t, with r as a decimal per year and t in years.
Percentage points: a rate going from 20% to 25% rose 5 percentage points, which is a 5 ÷ 20 = 25% relative increase.
Percent change = (new − original) ÷ original × 100%. Always divide by the ORIGINAL.
Discount: × (1 − rate). Tax or markup: × (1 + rate). Tip or commission alone: × rate.
Successive percents multiply: 20% off then 10% off = 28% off.
To undo a percent, divide by the multiplier: $64 after 20% off came from 64 ÷ 0.80 = $80.
Simple interest I = Prt. Percentage points are a difference of rates, not a percent change.

summary: You can now calculate percent increase and decrease from the original value, apply discounts, tax, tips and markups with multipliers, and chain successive percents correctly. You can also reverse a percent to find an original price, compute simple interest, and tell percentage points from percent change.

A.q: A clinic's monthly supply cost rose from $1,250 to $1,400. What was the percent increase? Round to the nearest tenth if needed.

whyNot.0: 10.7% divides the change by the new value (150 ÷ 1,400).
whyNot.2: 112% is the new cost as a percent of the old (1.12); the increase is the 12% above 100%.
whyNot.3: 1.2% moves the decimal only one place when converting 0.12.

A.q: Scrubs normally cost $56 and are on sale for 30% off. What is the sale price?

whyNot.0: $16.80 is the discount itself, not the price after the discount.
whyNot.3: $72.80 adds 30% instead of taking it off (56 × 1.30).

A.q: A dinner bill is $64.50. Rosa leaves an 18% tip on the bill. What is the total she pays, bill plus tip?

whyNot.0: $11.61 is the tip alone; the question asks for the total paid.
whyNot.2: $180.60 uses 1.8 for 18% (a tip of $116.10), a decimal-place slip.

B.q: A patient's weight dropped from 220 lb to 187 lb over six months. What was the percent decrease? Round to the nearest tenth if needed.
B.why: Change: 220 − 187 = 33. Divide by the original: 33 ÷ 220 = 0.15 = 15%. Check: 220 × 0.85 = 187. ✓

whyNot.1: 17.6% divides the change by the new weight (33 ÷ 187).
whyNot.2: 85% is the new weight as a percent of the old; the decrease is 100% − 85%.
whyNot.3: 33% treats the 33-lb change as a percent without dividing by the original.

B.q: A $250 stethoscope is marked 20% off, and a coupon takes an extra 15% off the sale price. What is the final price?

whyNot.0: $162.50 adds the discounts to 35% off. The coupon applies to the $200 sale price, not to $250.
whyNot.1: $87.50 is 35% of $250, a discount amount built on the added percents.
whyNot.2: $212.50 applies the 15% coupon and skips the 20% sale.

B.q: A textbook costs $84 before a 6.5% sales tax. What is the total cost with tax?

whyNot.1: $5.46 is the tax alone, not the total cost.
whyNot.3: $138.60 uses 1.65 as the multiplier, treating 6.5% as 65%.

C.q: After a 25% discount, a home blood pressure monitor costs $45. What was the original price?
C.why: The sale price is 75% of the original: 0.75 × original = 45, so original = 45 ÷ 0.75 = 60. Check: 60 × 0.75 = 45. ✓

whyNot.0: $56.25 adds 25% of $45 back on. The discount was 25% of the original, not of the sale price.
whyNot.1: $33.75 takes another 25% off the sale price.
whyNot.2: $180.00 divides by 0.25, treating $45 as the discount rather than the price paid.

C.q: A pharmacy buys bandages for $6.40 a box, marks them up 45%, and later sells them at 20% off the marked price. What is the sale price? Round to the nearest cent.

whyNot.0: $8.00 nets the percents to a 25% markup (6.40 × 1.25). Successive percents multiply; they do not subtract.
whyNot.2: $9.28 is the marked price before the 20% discount.
whyNot.3: $2.88 is the markup amount alone (45% of $6.40).

C.q: A nursing program's first-time pass rate rose from 80% to 92%. Which statement is correct?
options: It rose 12 percentage points, a 12% increase
It rose 15 percentage points, a 12% increase
It rose 12 percentage points, a 15% increase
It rose 12 percentage points, a 13% increase
C.why: 92 − 80 = 12 percentage points. Relative change: 12 ÷ 80 = 0.15, a 15% increase.

whyNot.0: A 12-point rise is not a 12% increase: the relative change divides by the original 80.
whyNot.1: The rates differ by 12 points, not 15; and the relative change is 15%, not 12%.
whyNot.3: 13% divides by the new rate (12 ÷ 92); percent change uses the original.

reteach.title: A savings jar
reteach.question: You have $100 in a savings jar. You spend 10% of it, then add 10% of what is left. Are you back to $100? What does this tell you about percents of percents?

blocks.h: Each change uses the current amount
blocks.body: Start with $100. Spending 10% leaves $90. Gaining 10% back means 10% of $90, which is only $9, so you end at $99, not $100. Every percent change is measured from the amount you have at that moment. That is why discounts stack by multiplying, why a decrease is undone by dividing, and why percent change always divides by the original.

blocks.text: To get back from $90 to $100 you need a rise of 10 ÷ 90 = 11.1%, not 10%. Undo a percent by dividing by its multiplier, never by adding the same percent back.

explain.body: Percent change = (new − original) ÷ original × 100%. The base is always the starting value.

test.q: Enrollment in a CNA course fell from 160 students to 136. What was the percent decrease? Round to the nearest tenth if needed.
test.why: Change: 160 − 136 = 24. Divide by the original: 24 ÷ 160 = 0.15 = 15%. Check: 160 × 0.85 = 136. ✓

whyNot.1: 24% treats the change in students as a percent without dividing by the original.
whyNot.3: 85% is the new enrollment as a percent of the old, not the decrease.

explain.body: Discount: multiply by 1 − rate. Tax or markup: multiply by 1 + rate. A 15% discount keeps 85% of the price.

test.q: Which expression gives the price of a $90 item after a 15% discount?
test.why: A 15% discount leaves 85% of the price: 90 × 0.85 = 76.50.

whyNot.1: 90 × 0.15 gives the discount ($13.50), not the price after it.
whyNot.3: 90 × 1.15 adds 15%, as for a tax or markup.

explain.body: Two changes in a row multiply. A rise of 10% then a fall of 10% gives 1.10 × 0.90 = 0.99 of the start.

test.q: A medication's price rises 10% and then falls 10%. What is the overall effect on the original price?
test.why: 1.10 × 0.90 = 0.99, so the price ends at 99% of the original: a 1% decrease.

whyNot.0: The 10% fall is taken from the higher price, so it removes more than the rise added.
whyNot.2: The result, 0.99, is below 1, so the price went down, not up.
whyNot.3: 10% decrease ignores the first rise entirely.

explain.body: I = P × r × t: principal times the yearly rate (as a decimal) times the years. Add I to P for the total owed or earned.

test.q: Simone puts $3,500 in an account paying 5% simple interest per year. What is the total in the account after 4 years?

whyNot.0: $700.00 is the interest alone; the question asks for the total.
whyNot.2: $3,675.00 includes only one year of interest.
whyNot.3: $4,254.27 compounds the interest each year; simple interest is earned on the $3,500 only.
